title: Responsible AI for Official Statistics
text:
The aim of this training is to present the principles of responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in official statistics.
The materials cover ethical, methodological, technological and organisational aspects of using AI at different stages of the statistical process.
The training demonstrates how to make use of the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence while taking into account the limitations of AI models, data protection, the quality of results and accountability for decisions made.

title: Responsible AI for Official Statistics
text:
3 Summary
The responsible use of AI in official statistics requires combining statistical and technological expertise with appropriate oversight, data protection, transparency and systematic quality assessment.
The goal is not simply to implement new technologies, but to use them consciously wherever they can improve the quality, efficiency and reliability of the statistical process.

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
text:
GSBPM (Generic Statistical Business Process Model) organizes the activities leading from the identification of information needs to the evaluation of a statistical process.
The model helps identify where AI can support statistical production, as well as the risks and controls that must be considered at each stage.
Version 5.2 of the GSBPM was introduced in 2025 and serves as the current reference point for this module.

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
section: 3 3. AI in the Needs Identification Phase
text:
3 3. AI in the Needs Identification Phase
Artificial intelligence plays a key role in diagnosing and aggregating user needs. Thanks to its ability to instantly process huge volumes of qualitative and quantitative data, AI effectively supports the analysis of feedback, queries, and requests.
Example tasks:

topic clustering — categorizing collected feedback or questions to organize the main areas of discussion.
identification of recurring issues — catching the most frequently reported difficulties or challenges that require urgent attention.
preparation of a working consultation summary — creating an initial report with key conclusions and findings from the meeting.

The results require control because the frequency of a topic does not necessarily reflect its importance. A smaller group of users may report needs of high significance.

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
section: 4 4. AI in the Design and Build Phases
text:
4 4. AI in the Design and Build Phases
In the design and coding phases, artificial intelligence acts as an active assistant supporting the technical team. Its application covers key areas of the software lifecycle:

code prototyping: fast generation of application skeletons, UI components, SQL queries, or class structures, which shortens the time needed to write code from scratch and facilitates experimentation with different architectural approaches.
unit testing generation: automatic creation of test cases.
comparison of algorithmic methods and approaches: analysis of alternative technological solutions in terms of computational complexity, performance, and suitability for deployment in a given business context.
data flow documentation: automatic generation of function descriptions, architecture diagrams, and comments explaining the business logic contained in individual system modules.
identification of potential code issues: early detection of anti-patterns, syntax errors, security vulnerabilities, and areas requiring performance optimization.

Code generation should not be equated with correctness. Code requires testing, review, and verification of compliance with methodological requirements

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
section: 5 5. AI in Data Collection and Processing
text:
5 5. AI in Data Collection and Processing
The use of artificial intelligence in the collection and analysis of information significantly speeds up routine tasks, reduces errors, and raises the quality of managed resources.
Examples:

OCR and form field recognition: artificial intelligence analyzes scans or photos of documents (e.g., invoices, contracts, ID cards), extracting text (Optical Character Recognition) and mapping it to appropriate system fields (e.g., NIP, date, gross amount).
classification of text descriptions: automatic assignment of categories, tags, or codes to unstructured text data (e.g., customer comments, service requests, emails), facilitating their routine routing and analysis.
detection of unusual records (anomalies): algorithms analyze patterns and trends in historical data to indicate transactions, entries, or behaviors that drastically deviate from the norm (e.g., potential system errors or fraud attempts).
data editing support: systems supporting the user during data entry (so-called smart autocomplete or contextual hints) that suggest correct values based on previously entered information or reference dictionaries.
imputation of missing values: the use of statistical models and machine learning to intelligently fill in gaps in databases based on correlations between other available variables.

In each of these situations, it is necessary to determine whether AI only proposes a result or can automatically change data. It is worth keeping information about the origin of a value and whether it was observed, corrected, or imputed.

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
text:
6 6. AI in Analysis and Dissemination
AI tools can support the team in particular in the following areas:

anomaly and trend search: rapid scanning of large datasets for unusual changes, deviations from the norm, or hidden correlations.
preliminary interpretation of results: preparation of working hypotheses and draft versions of descriptions that facilitate further analytical work.
drafting publications: editing the first versions of text descriptions intended for reports, articles, or press materials.
designing visualizations: generating proposals for optimal forms of graphical data presentation (e.g., chart types or infographics).
documentation navigation: instant retrieval of definitions, indicators, and guidelines in extensive methodological knowledge bases.

Final conclusions must be consistent with the results and methodology. Text generated by a model is not statistical evidence in itself.

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
text:
7 7. Cross-Cutting Controls
Not all issues can be assigned to a single GSBPM phase. Some safeguards should cover the entire solution lifecycle:

data protection and security: ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and security of processed information at every operational stage.
documentation and versioning: systematic recording of changes in code, models, datasets, and documentation of design assumptions.
validation and monitoring: continuous verification of correct model operation, data drift detection, and ongoing tracking of quality metrics.
access management: control of permissions and authorization of users and systems in contact with AI data and models.
human oversight: maintaining operational control and the ability for human intervention at key decision-making moments by the system.
risk management: identification, mitigation, and ongoing assessment of ethical, legal, and technical risks.
training and competencies: raising awareness and qualifications of teams responsible for the development, implementation, and maintenance of the system.

When planning the application of AI, dependencies between phases should also be taken into account. Errors made at early stages (e.g., imprecise problem formulation or imperfections in data collection and cleaning) often remain invisible during the training phase and only become apparent in advanced stages of analysis, testing, or directly after publishing the solution.

title: The Application of AI in the GSBPM Statistical Process
text:
8 8. Process Example: Tourism Data Imputation
Suppose an office wants to predict the number of tourists for establishments that failed to submit a report on time.

Needs Identification: determining whether a previous result is needed to prepare preliminary statistical information.
Design: selection of variables, predictors, and validation method.
Build: preparation of code, tests, and environment.
Collection: acquisition of reporting data and auxiliary information.
Processing: data control and generating imputation.
Analysis: comparison of results with actual observations and the baseline method.
Dissemination: preparation of results with appropriate status description and limitations.
Evaluation: assessment of the quality and usefulness of the solution and decision on changes.

In practice, processes are rarely purely linear – individual phases can repeat, intertwine, and occur in variable order.

AI can support many GSBPM phases, but its application should stem from a specific need.
Risk depends on the role of the result in the process, not just the type of algorithm.
Controls should cover the entire solution lifecycle.
GSBPM can be used to locate AI applications, document them, and plan quality assessment.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
AI systems can process data locally, within an institution’s infrastructure, or through external services. Depending on the solution, input data, prompts, files, logs, and outputs may be subject to different retention and access rules.
In public statistics, protecting individual data, including data obtained through statistical surveys, is of paramount importance. The improper use of AI can lead to the disclosure of confidential information, violation of access rules, or loss of control over how data is processed.
Security does not depend solely on whether a tool is well-known or popular. Its configuration, terms of service, scope of permissions, the type of data transferred, and approved organizational procedures are essential.
The objective of this module is to prepare participants to identify risks and choose a safe method for using AI.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
3.2 Disclosure via Prompt or Attachment
Confidential data can be passed to an AI model not only in the main query content, but also in an attachment, code snippet, error message, screenshot, or problem description.
Example: an employee asks the model to fix R code and attaches a data snippet containing unit identifiers.
The most common channels for unintentional leaks include:

Source code snippets: Pasting scripts containing real variable names, paths to internal statistical office databases, or unit identifiers.
Error messages and logs: Copying messages from a developer console that contain table names and specific records on which the error occurred.
Screenshots and images: Uploading photos or screenshots, as multimodal models process all visible text in the image, including confidential background data.
Attached files: Attaching documents containing hidden sheets, metadata, or raw microdata cached in pivot tables.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
section: 3.3 Prompt Attacks (Prompt Injection, Hijacking, and Jailbreaking)
text:
3.3 Prompt Attacks (Prompt Injection, Hijacking, and Jailbreaking)

Prompt Injection: Injecting malicious instructions into an analyzed file (e.g., in a respondent survey), enticing the model to break procedures.
Prompt Leaking: Forcing the disclosure of system instructions or confidential metadata contained in the context.
Jailbreaking: Bypassing built-in safety filters using complex storytelling or logical prompts.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
3.4 Excessive Permissions
An AI assistant or agent may gain access to documents, databases, or systems far broader than necessary to accomplish the task. The principle of least privilege requires that the tool and user possess access solely to the resources essential for achieving a specific goal.
To secure access, it is advisable to implement permission inheritance, a default read-only mode, and execution of AI-generated scripts in isolated environments.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
3.5 Unauthorized Disclosure in Responses
The system may place a fragment of a confidential document, data from an incorrect source, or information accessible to the user only in a different context into its response.
The main risks stem primarily from bypassing permissions, when AI responds based on files inaccessible to a given user. Furthermore, a threat arises from context mixing and hallucinations, during which the model may weave fragments from unpublished reports or internal documents into a public response.
To effectively prevent leaks in responses, output filters should be implemented to automatically scan responses for data, enforce permission checks so the search engine searches only files accessible to the given user, and verify AI-generated responses prior to further dissemination.

section: 3.6 Loss of Control over Documentation and Results

text:
3.7 Adversarial Attacks and Data Poisoning
Deliberate, human-imperceptible modification of input data in order to mislead the ML model.
Inserting manipulated records into a training dataset to secretly bias statistical results.
The risk of malicious code present in downloaded open-source models.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
3.8 Data Extraction from Training Sets

Membership Inference Attacks: Techniques allowing an attacker to determine whether specific subject data was used in the training process.
Model Inversion & Reconstruction Attacks: Analysis of model responses allowing partial reconstruction of unique source records.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
4.1 Anonymization
Anonymization is a process aimed at irreversibly preventing the identification of a person or entity from data, taking into account all means that can reasonably be used.
Simply removing direct identifiers (such as first name, last name, or personal identification number) does not guarantee full anonymization. Identification may still be possible by combining remaining information, for example, location, age, occupation, and a rare characteristic.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
4.2 Pseudonymization
Pseudonymization consists of processing personal or individual data in such a way that it can no longer be attributed to a specific person or entity without the use of an additional linkage key. This key must be stored separately and secured organizationally and technically.
Pseudonymized data can still constitute personal data. Pseudonymization should not be treated as automatic authorization to transfer data to external AI tools.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
4.3 Synthetic Data
Synthetic data is artificially generated, for example, for code testing or solution prototyping.
It can reduce the need to use real data, but does not guarantee the absence of disclosure risk. If the generator reproduces distinctive observations from the source dataset, an additional risk assessment may be necessary.
Good practice: Prototyping code on artificial data with a similar structure, followed by validation in an approved environment.
Bad practice: Considering data anonymous solely because identifiers have been removed.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
section: 5.1 Example: Assistance in Writing R Code
text:
5.1 Example: Assistance in Writing R Code
An employee wants assistance with joining two datasets.
Inappropriate approach:
Sending complete files containing individual data, identifiers, and confidential information.
Safer approach:

Prepares a small, synthetic example showing column structure.
Replaces real values with dummy data.
Formulates the problem without revealing protected information.
Tests the generated code in an approved environment.
Verifies the correctness of results on data to which authorized access is granted.

If the problem cannot be reproduced on synthetic data, an approved environment and proper consultation procedure should be used.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
6.1 Prompt Injection
Prompt injection involves attempting to influence the model’s behavior through input content, for example, a document or webpage containing instructions intended to induce the system to violate established rules.
Example: an assistant searches for answers in documents, and one of them contains an instruction to reveal other accessible files.
Document content should be treated as material for analysis, not as automatically trusted system instructions.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
6.3 Integration with Documentation
An assistant utilizing RAG should have restricted access to approved documents, respect user permissions, and cite answer sources.
It is not enough that the model can find a document. It is also necessary to check whether it discloses fragments of documents to which the user should not have access.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
6.4 Guardrails
Special protective layers are applied to secure model integration with external systems. They act as input and output filters for the AI system.

6.4.1 The Role of Input and Output Filters

Input filter: Checks the user’s query or analyzed document before passing it to the model. Blocks Prompt Injection attack attempts, detects personal data, and rejects unauthorized queries.
Output filter: Verifies the response generated by the model before displaying it to a human. Checks whether the response complies with the schema (e.g., valid JSON format), contains no hallucinations, and has not disseminated confidential data.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
7.1 Data Minimization
The data minimization principle requires applying the Necessity and Proportionality test.
In practice, this means:

Sending schema instead of data: If you need help writing a script, do not send a file with real records. Providing column names and variable types is sufficient.
Filtering and trimming scope: If the model must analyze a text snippet or table, remove all columns, rows, and metadata from the file that are not directly related to the task.
Aggregation instead of microdata: If the problem concerns trend analysis at the voivodeship (regional) level, do not send records concerning specific companies or households; send exclusively aggregated data (sums, averages).
Prototyping on synthetic data: Perform all testing, prompt engineering practice, and code development on dummy data. Attach real data only within a secured environment.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
7.2 Principle of Least Privilege
This principle applies both to employees and to AI tools and systems themselves. An AI assistant or agent should see and do only as much as a specific task requires of it.
In practice, this means:

Restricting model rights: An AI system analyzing documents should not have the capability to modify databases, send emails, or delete files. By default, it should hold read-only permissions.
Environment isolation: Conducting experiments, writing scripts, and testing AI models should occur in isolated environments using test data. The production environment containing sensitive data must be strictly separated.
Reflecting user permissions in RAG: If an AI assistant searches an internal agency knowledge base, it must not display a response from a document to which the employee does not have direct access rights in official agency systems.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
7.3 Data Retention and Storage Duration
Minimization also applies to the length of time data remains within an AI system:

Limiting log retention duration: Prompts, attachments, and outputs should not be stored in external AI service memory longer than necessary to generate the response.
Automated temporary file cleanup: Databases and models should not accumulate redundant query copies. Upon ending a working session, temporary files should be removed.

title: Module 3. Data Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security
text:
9.1 Proposed Solution

A: Typically low risk of data disclosure, as no individual data is transferred. Approved tool usage guidelines should still be followed.
B: Data should not be transferred until confirming that the tool and processing method are permitted. Removing a few identifiers does not necessarily resolve the issue.
C: Typically a good approach for prototyping, provided that synthetic data does not disclose information from the actual dataset.
D: Permissions should be restricted to resources essential for task execution, and verification should confirm whether the system respects individual user permissions.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) create new opportunities for official statistics. They can support data processing, automation of repetitive tasks, missing value imputation, information classification, alternative data analysis, and the preparation of result descriptions.
At the same time, the use of these technologies entails new challenges. A result generated by a model may be erroneous, incomplete, biased, or difficult to explain. Data provided to an external tool may be subject to unwanted disclosure. Automation can also make it difficult to determine who is responsible for a decision and how the result was produced.
In official statistics, the consequences of such problems extend beyond a single analytical error. They can affect the quality of published data, the interpretation of social and economic phenomena, and public trust in official statistics.
Therefore, responsible use of AI should not be understood solely as compliance with IT security rules. It encompasses the entire process: from defining the objective of application, through the selection of data and methods, to validation, interpretation, dissemination of results, and monitoring of the solution.
The module uses as key reference points materials from the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), in particular the Responsible AI for Official Statistics Framework (2025), Generative AI for Official Statistics (2025), the publication Ethics in Official Statistics (2026), and the UN Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
3.1 Accountability vs. Technical Correctness
Three levels of evaluation for a solution should be distinguished:







Level
Example Question




Technical Correctness
Does the code execute without error?


Methodological Correctness
Is the applied method appropriate for the objective, and have the results been properly verified?


Responsible Use
Is the application justified, secure, transparent, and subject to appropriate oversight?



A positive evaluation at one level does not guarantee a positive evaluation at the others.
For example, a model may generate results with low prediction error but systematically overestimate values for a specific group of units. Code may run correctly but remove a portion of observations in a way that contradicts study assumptions. Conversely, a tool may be technically secure, but its application may lack sufficient methodological justification.
Conclusion: trust in official statistics is built on adherence to professional standards, scientific integrity, and ethical considerations. Implementing responsible AI requires rigorous and transparent methodologies that guarantee quality at every stage: data collection, processing, storage, and presentation.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
4.1 Key Features of Official Statistics

4.1.1 1. Public Trust
Users must have a justified conviction that statistics are compiled based on sound methods and that the way they are prepared does not unduly favor specific interests.
The use of AI should not make it harder to demonstrate that the statistical production process remains under the institution control.


4.1.2 2. Statistical Quality
High algorithmic efficacy is not synonymous with high statistical quality. Depending on the application, considerations must include, among others:

accuracy and reliability of results;
consistency with the adopted methodology;
comparability over time and space;
timeliness;
completeness;
uncertainty of results;
impact of the method applied on statistical indicators and aggregates.



4.1.3 3. Confidentiality
Microdata collected for statistical purposes require special protection. The use of AI does not remove the obligation to maintain confidentiality, nor does it justify automatically transferring data to any arbitrary tool.


4.1.4 4. Impartiality and Professional Independence
Statistical methods and procedures should be selected based on professional and scientific criteria.
An AI solution should not be adopted simply because it is trendy, vendor-recommended, or organizationally expected. Its usefulness should be evaluated relative to a specific statistical problem.


4.1.5 5. Transparency and Accountability
The organization should be able to explain how AI was used, what data and methods were applied, how result quality was evaluated, and who is responsible for process oversight.
The scope of documentation and explanation should be tailored to the nature and risk of the given application.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
section: 6.2 Example: Automated Draft Comments on Results
text:
6.2 Example: Automated Draft Comments on Results
A generative model prepares a description of the growth in the number of enterprises based on a statistical table.
Even if the model uses aggregated data exclusively, it may attribute changes to the wrong cause, confuse reference periods, or exaggerate the significance of a minor difference.
Responsible use therefore requires verifying not only the consistency of the text with the table, but also whether the narrative goes beyond what is legitimately supported by the data.
Conclusion: evaluating an AI application should include at least three questions:

Is the action compliant with applicable regulations and institutional rules?
Is it methodologically justified?
Are its consequences acceptable from the perspective of professional ethics and public trust?

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
7.1 Potential Benefits

Efficiency: reduction of time-consuming, repetitive tasks.
Scalability: ability to process large datasets and numerous documents.
Analytical support: identification of patterns and anomalies that would be difficult to detect manually.
New data sources: supporting the analysis of text data and other alternative sources.
Better documentation: supporting the creation of method descriptions, code, and user guides.
Information accessibility: facilitating search and explanation of statistical publication content.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
7.2 Key Risks

Errors and hallucinations: generation of false information or faulty code.
Bias: uneven result quality across different groups of units.
Loss of confidentiality: improper data transmission or disclosure of confidential information.
Lack of transparency: difficulty explaining how results were produced and inability to fully trace the model reasoning path.
Over-automation: reduction of expert oversight.
Vendor lock-in: difficulties in reproducing the process or switching tools.
Quality degradation over time: deterioration of model performance following changes in data or conditions.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
section: 8.1 Case A: Code Generation for Data Cleaning
text:
8.1 Case A: Code Generation for Data Cleaning
Situation
An analyst uses a generative model to prepare R code that standardizes column names, removes duplicates, and joins data from several files.
Bad practice
The analyst copies the code into a production script because it executes without error. They do not verify whether the post-processing record count matches expectations or whether information was lost during column joins.
Good practice
The analyst:

Tests the code on a small, controlled dataset.
Checks record counts and data structure before and after processing.
Verifies how missing values, duplicates, and conflicting values are handled.
Compares results with an independently prepared control example.
Documents significant changes and maintains process reproducibility.

Conclusion
AI can speed up programming, but it does not replace testing or responsibility for data processing logic.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
section: 8.2 Case B: Forecasting Model for Statistical Results
text:
8.2 Case B: Forecasting Model for Statistical Results
Situation
A team builds a model to forecast the number of tourists staying in accommodation establishments.
Bad practice
The model achieves low training error. The team considers it superior and deploys it without comparison to a baseline method, without temporal validation, and without evaluating regional performance.
Good practice
The team:

Compares the model against reasonable baseline methods.
Evaluates performance on out-of-sample data unused for fitting.
Applies a split that respects observational chronology.
Analyzes errors across key statistical breakdowns.
Checks result stability across different periods.
Defines guidelines for monitoring and re-evaluating the model.

Conclusion
Model quality should be evaluated under conditions corresponding to actual future deployment, not solely on training data.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
8.3 Case C: AI Documentation Assistant
Situation
An organizational unit creates an assistant to answer questions about procedures, methodology, and guidelines.
Bad practice
The assistant answers questions without citing sources. If the AI model does not provide sources, the employee cannot tell whether the answer is based on official office guidelines or invented by the algorithm from general web content.
Good practice
The solution uses vetted documents, cites answer sources, flags when information is insufficient, and is tested on ambiguous questions to ensure it cannot be easily misled.
Conclusion
Faster workflows carry no value if bought at the risk of error. An AI assistant is valuable only when a human can rapidly and independently verify the truthfulness of the provided answer.

title: Module 1. Specifics of Responsible AI in Official Statistics
text:
8.4 Case D: Microdata Processing
Situation
An employee wants to accelerate microdata analysis by sending a slice of a dataset to a publicly available AI tool.
Bad practice
The employee assumes that limiting the record count is sufficient to ensure security.
Good practice
The employee uses an approved environment, checks the permissibility of the planned processing, minimizes data scope, and consults uncertainties with data protection and security officers.
Conclusion
Security depends on data type, processing method, and tool usage terms, not merely on dataset size.

10.2 Tasks for Participant

Identify at least three benefits of using the tool.
Identify at least four risks.
Determine which risks could directly impact the credibility of published statistics.
Propose a minimum set of controls prior to deployment.
Decide whether the tool can be deployed in its current form.



Proposed Solution

Potential benefits:

shorter drafting time;
standardization of initial descriptions;
reduction of repetitive tasks.

Key risks:

confusing reference periods;
misinterpreting the direction or scale of change;
attributing unjustified causes;
lack of uniform content oversight;
risk of publishing an erroneous description.

Recommended controls:

Automated checks of reference periods, units, and numerical values.
Restricting generation of causes unbacked by data and approved sources.
Testing on a set of correct, ambiguous, and difficult test cases.
Mandatory substantive verification prior to publication.
Error logging and regular quality evaluation.

Decision: in its current form, the tool should not independently prepare texts for publication without human review. The pilot may continue, or the tool may be allowed as a drafting assistant, provided appropriate safeguards are implemented.

title: Generative AI in official statistics
text:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) creates new content based on patterns learned during training and information provided in a given task.
Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate and transform text, explain code, summarize documents, and support information retrieval.
However, this does not mean that every answer is true, up-to-date, or based on a reliable source.
From a transparency perspective, an LLM is a typical black-box model: it processes data through many layers of transformations that are difficult to trace. In contrast, white-box models (e.g., linear regression, decision trees) are inherently interpretable. In practice, this means that a tester has full access to the documentation, source code, and configuration.

What it means in practice

The system does not worsen the situation of any group


Privacy and security
Data and models are protected


Validity and robustness
Results are reliable even outside the test set

section: 6 6. How to prepare a good prompt?
text:
6 6. How to prepare a good prompt?
A useful prompt specifies:

Goal — what needs to be done?
Context — which process does the task relate to?
Scope — what should the model not do?
Output format — table, list, code, or description.
Quality criteria — what constitutes a correct result?
Verification — how to indicate uncertainty and lack of information?

Example:

Prepare a draft description for the statistical table. Use only the values provided below. Do not infer the causes of the observed changes. Separate the description of facts from interpretation. If there is not enough data to formulate a conclusion, explicitly state this.

Only information whose use is permitted in a given tool should be passed in the prompt.

title: Generative AI in official statistics
text:
7 7. RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) combines a generative model with information retrieval from a specific set of documents.
Typical workflow:

The user asks a question.
The system searches for relevant document fragments.
The selected fragments are passed to the model.
The model prepares an answer based on them.
The user can check the cited sources.

RAG can mitigate some problems arising from a lack of context, but it does not guarantee the truthfulness of the answer. The system may retrieve wrong fragments, misinterpret them, or omit important information.
The quality of the index, the currency of the documents, access rights, and the verifiability of cited sources are important.
In a RAG system, it is also worth taking care of data provenance (where the document comes from, who is responsible for it, how it is updated) and the audit trail: a record of which fragments were used for the answer.

title: Generative AI in official statistics
text:
8 8. Safe use of GenAI
Before using a tool, check:

whether it is approved for a given type of task;
whether data used in the task can be passed to it;
whether the prompt is free of confidential information;
whether the output does not reveal protected data or information;
whether the answer has been verified before use;
whether restrictions on saving and retaining data apply.

A public AI interface should not automatically be treated as a safe place to process official business data.

8.1 Common threats to ML models







Threat
What it entails




Adversarial attack
Intentional manipulation of input data to make the model fail


Data poisoning
Injecting flawed data into the training set


Model inversion
Reconstructing fragments of training data from model outputs


Membership inference
Determining whether a given entity was in the training set


Insider threats
Abuse of access rights by employees


Transfer learning risk
Transfer of residual information or “backdoors” from another model



Countermeasures include data validation and sanitization, restricting model access, anomaly monitoring, regular updates, and privacy-enhancing technologies (e.g., differential privacy, federated learning). Data minimization, privacy impact assessments, and employee training are also crucial.

title: Generative AI in official statistics
text:
9 9. Prompt injection and untrusted content
A document, webpage, or other material processed by a model may contain instructions that attempt to change the system’s behavior.
For example, a document might contain text ordering the disclosure of confidential information or the ignoring of previous rules.
Content retrieved from a document should be treated as material for analysis, not as authorization to change how the system operates.
In systems that use tools, files, or automated actions, permissions should be restricted, sources verified, and confirmation required for actions with significant consequences.
This is an example of a broader rule: an AI system should not act autonomously where its actions have real-world consequences, and a human must retain effective oversight.

12 12. Accountability, oversight, and review
“Algorithms are not accountable, someone is accountable for the algorithms.” In practice, this means:

assigning roles – who is responsible for development, deployment, and monitoring;
impact and risk assessment at an early stage, with higher requirements for higher-risk applications;
auditability – decision trail, versioning, possibility of review by independent persons;
appeal mechanism for individuals affected by the results.

Example review process (based on Statistics Canada):

Self-assessment by the team using a checklist.
Peer review – ethical and methodological, by independent experts.
Scientific committee – approval and recommendations, especially for new methods or key statistical programs.
Publication of a review report (or its summary if full disclosure is impossible).

A generative model was instructed to prepare a commentary for a table. In response, it provided three reasons for the increase in the indicator’s value, although the table only contains values for consecutive years.
Answer the following questions:

Which elements of the answer can be verified based on the table?
What information is missing to determine the causes?
How should the prompt be modified?
How should the verification of the generated text be documented?
Who should approve the commentary before publication and on what basis?

Hint: distinguish the description of changes from the explanation of their causes. Data on values alone does not prove causality.

title: Checklists
text:
1 How to use the checklists
Checklists help verify whether the most important issues have been taken into account in an AI project. They do not replace a formal risk assessment, consultation with the data protection officer, or the procedures in force in the organisation.
The checklists are arranged in an order similar to the successive stages of a project: from defining the objective, through data and the model, to deployment and monitoring. List 8 concerns generative AI tools and should be taken into account whenever such tools are used. The checklists are best completed as a team, with the involvement of those responsible for the project, the data and the methodology. For each “Yes” answer, it is worth noting where the supporting evidence can be found, e.g. in the documentation, a validation report or the outcomes of a meeting.
Answers:

Yes — the requirement has been met and evidence can be provided.
No — the requirement has not been met.
Not applicable — the requirement does not apply; it is worth briefly explaining why.

“No” answers should be analysed before moving on to the next stage of the project.


2 List 1. Purpose and justification for using AI
This list is used to check whether, at the start of the project, it has been clearly defined what problem the system is meant to solve and why AI is a suitable tool for it. It also helps establish who will use the results, what the success criteria are and who is responsible for the project. It is worth completing first, before work on the data and the model begins.

The problem that the system is meant to solve has been defined.
It has been justified why AI is an appropriate solution.
Simpler alternatives have been considered, e.g. rules, classical statistical methods or automation.
The users and the recipients of the results have been identified.
It has been determined how the results will be used.
Success criteria and acceptable error have been defined.
The consequences of an incorrect result have been identified.
The person responsible for the project and the person approving the results have been named.

Review outcome: the project’s purpose and the justification for using AI are documented.


3 List 2. Data, confidentiality and security
This list concerns the data used in the project: its origin, quality, the permissions to use it, and its protection. It pays particular attention to personal and confidential data, including individual-level data covered by statistical confidentiality. It is completed before data processing begins and updated whenever the sources or scope of the data change.

The sources, scope and origin of the data have been determined.
The permissions to use the data for the given purpose have been checked.
Personal data, confidential data and other protected information have been identified.
The risk of identifying persons or units has been assessed.
The scope of the processed data has been limited to the necessary minimum.
The quality, completeness and timeliness of the data have been verified.
The representativeness of the data for the intended use has been checked.
Rules for data access, storage and deletion have been established.
It has been verified whether the use of external tools is permitted.
The procedure to follow in the event of an incident has been defined.

Review outcome: the manner in which the data is obtained and processed complies with the requirements applicable to the project.


4 List 3. Model validation and quality
This list makes it possible to assess whether the model has been properly tested and whether its quality is sufficient for the intended use. It covers the data split, the choice of validation method and quality measures, comparison with a baseline method, and a description of the model’s limitations. It also includes additional questions for projects that use time series, e.g. forecasts. It is completed once the model has been built, before a decision is made to use it.

A method for splitting the data into training, validation and test sets has been defined.
The risk of information leakage between the sets has been eliminated.
A validation method appropriate to the purpose and the data structure has been applied.
The model has been compared with a baseline method.
Quality measures appropriate to the intended use have been selected.
Errors have been analysed for relevant groups and areas.
The behaviour of the model in atypical situations has been checked.
The stability of the results has been assessed.
Limitations and known weaknesses have been documented.
The conditions for approving the model for use have been defined.

Additional questions for time series:

Does the model use only information available at the time the forecast is made?
Does the test take into account the actual chronological order?
Have errors been checked in different periods, including atypical ones?



5 List 4. Bias and fairness
This list helps check whether the model performs similarly for different groups, e.g. regions, age groups or types of units, and whether it leads to unjustified differences in results. It draws attention to group sizes, data quality and the consequences of errors for individual recipients. It is best completed in parallel with the assessment of model quality.

Groups for which the model may perform differently have been identified.
The number of observations in these groups has been checked.
The quality of results has been compared across groups.
The impact of missing data and of the method used to impute it has been analysed.
It has been checked whether input features lead to unjustified differentiation of results.
The consequences of errors for individual users or areas have been assessed.
The limitations identified and the remedial actions have been documented.

Not every difference between groups indicates bias. Such a difference does, however, require analysis in the context of the model’s purpose, the quality of the data and the consequences of its use.


6 List 5. Transparency and documentation
This list concerns whether the solution is described in a way that allows other people to understand it, reproduce it and use it appropriately. It covers documentation of the purpose, data, method, code and model versions, test results, and information for recipients. It is worth updating on an ongoing basis during the project, rather than only at its end.

The purpose, scope and limitations of the model have been documented.
The data sources and their preparation have been described.
The method used and the justification for choosing it have been recorded.
The version of the code, the model and the significant dependencies have been recorded.
The validation method and the test results have been documented.
Known limitations and cases in which the model should not be used have been defined.
Information on how to interpret the results has been prepared.
A way of informing recipients about the use of AI has been established, if required or appropriate.



7 List 6. Human oversight
This list is used to check whether the model’s results remain under human control and whether it is clear who verifies them, and in what situations. It concerns, among other things, procedures for handling atypical results, the possibility of challenging a result, and the reporting of errors. It is completed before deployment, and revisited whenever the way the model is used changes.

A person responsible for oversight has been designated.
It has been determined which results require human verification.
A procedure for handling atypical results has been established.
The people using the model are aware of its limitations.
It is possible to challenge or reject the model’s result.
Decisions with significant consequences are not taken without the required review.
A way of reporting errors and incidents has been defined.



8 List 7. Deployment and monitoring
This list concerns preparing for the launch of the solution and its subsequent maintenance. It helps establish the conditions for deployment, the way quality will be monitored, the rules for updating and re-validation, and a plan for withdrawing the model if necessary. It is completed before deployment and repeated during periodic reviews.

The deployment conditions and acceptance criteria have been defined.
Indicators for monitoring quality have been established.
The frequency of reviews has been determined.
Warning thresholds and the actions to take when they are exceeded have been defined.
Changes in data distributions and in the quality of input data are monitored.
The reproducibility of results has been ensured.
Rules for updating and re-validating the model have been defined.
The possibility of withdrawing the model or reverting to the baseline method has been planned.
Responsibility for maintaining the solution has been assigned.



9 List 8. Generative AI
This list concerns the responsible use of generative AI tools, e.g. for creating texts, code or summaries. It draws attention to whether the tool is approved for use, the protection of the data entered into it, and the obligation for a human to check and approve the generated content. It is worth applying whenever such tools are used in work, including outside large projects.

The tool is approved for the intended use.
No prohibited data is entered into the tool.
Generated code is reviewed and tested.
Generated content is verified for substantive accuracy.
Figures, sources, quotations and references are checked.
Verified content is distinguished from suggestions generated by the model.
The use of AI is documented where necessary.
Responsibility for approved results is not attributed to the model.



10 Review summary
Once the lists have been completed, a short note should be prepared covering:

the name and purpose of the solution;
the date of the review;
the persons taking part in the assessment;
requirements that have not been met or that need improvement;
corrective actions, the persons responsible and deadlines;
the decision on whether to approve the solution for the next stage.

A checklist supports the risk management process; it is not an automatic certificate of compliance.

title: Validation and monitoring of AI systems
text:
Validation is checking whether a model provides reliable results in the application for which it is to be used, which also means on data it did not see during training.
It is not enough for a model to perform well on the data it was built on. In official statistics, it is about valid inference: the results must be reliable, and their accuracy known, as they form the basis for public decisions and policies.
In the context of machine learning, validation means evaluating whether:

the model generalizes well to new, previously unseen observations;
the quality from the training and evaluation stage is maintained in the inference phase, i.e., in practical use;
the model performs well for observations from the same population, but over a longer period.












Application
Example validation question
Example method




Activity classification
Does the model also recognize rare or new types of activity well?
Test on data outside the training set, error analysis in subgroups


Missing value imputation
Are the imputed values close to the true ones?
Hiding known values and comparing with the model’s output


Forecasting
Does the model work well in the period following the training data?
Chronological validation and comparison with a naive forecast


Text coding
Is the quality similar for different sources and types of descriptions?
Comparison with manual coding on a control sample






A model assigns activity descriptions to categories. On the test set, it achieves 94% correct classifications, so it looks good.
However, validation asks further questions:

Is the result equally good for small and rare categories?
Is it better only because the test data was too similar to the training data?
Does the simpler, existing method yield similar results?
Will the quality drop when descriptions in new submissions change?





It is not a one-time test before launch. It is a process that continues throughout the model’s life cycle.
It does not boil down to a single metric. High overall accuracy can hide poor results in important subgroups.
It does not solely concern the model. It encompasses the entire process: data collection, processing, feature engineering, training, and prediction.

title: Validation and monitoring of AI systems
text:
2 2. Why is validation necessary?
A model that achieved good results during development may not perform equally well on new data.
In official statistics, erroneous results can affect the quality of publications, data comparability over time, and the reliability of information.
Validation should answer three questions:

Does the model work well enough?
Does it work well for different periods and groups?
Does its quality remain acceptable after deployment?

This is of particular importance when model predictions feed into a process leading to population-level estimators. Then the model must not only be accurate but also reliable, and the data user should know how reliable the published numbers are.

title: Validation and monitoring of AI systems
text:
3 3. Three stages of evaluation








Stage
When
Main question




Pre-deployment validation
During model development
Is the model good enough and correctly implemented?


Pre-use validation
Before each use of outputs
Do the conditions of use correspond to those for which the model was approved?


Post-deployment monitoring
While the model is running
Do quality and data remain stable?




3.1 3.1. Pre-deployment validation
Goal: make sure the model is correct and fit for purpose before it goes into production.
Includes:

checking data quality;
evaluating assumptions and implementation correctness;
testing on data not used for training;
comparison with a baseline method;
error and edge case analysis.

Validation covers the entire workflow: data collection, preprocessing, feature engineering, training, and prediction. You need to check the representativeness and quality of training data, limit biases and confounding factors, and maintain consistency across all stages.
The transition from a prototype to a production version is a good time for a formal review (see Section 13).


3.2 3.2. Pre-use validation
Goal: confirm that the model is used under the conditions for which it was approved.
Includes checking whether the input data and operating conditions correspond to those for which the model was approved.


3.3 3.3. Post-deployment monitoring
Goal: detect quality degradation and changing conditions before they affect published results.
Includes observing:

output quality;
changes in input data;
result stability;
the occurrence of unexpected situations.

text:
5 5. Choice of metrics







Task
Example metrics




Regression
MAE, RMSE, MASE


Classification
Precision, Recall, F1, confusion matrix


Imbalanced classes
Precision, Recall, PR-AUC


Forecasting
MAE, RMSE, MASE and comparison with a baseline forecast


Imputation
Imputation error on known values and subgroup evaluation



A model should not be chosen solely based on a single metric.
For instance, RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily than MAE. When evaluating imputation, it is also worth checking if the errors are systematic and if their distribution differs between groups.
ML metrics are not everything. Measures calculated on a test or validation set may not reflect reliability in production. Therefore, when model outputs feed official statistics, they should be supplemented with statistical quality indicators (e.g., coefficient of variation, uncertainty measures), which inform users about the reliability of estimators.
Metrics in subgroups. If a model affects population groups or different types of entities, measures must also be calculated in subgroups and an acceptable level of difference defined. The limitations of the chosen measures must be clearly described, as it is impossible to satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously.

8 8. Drift and changing conditions
Various types of changes can occur after deployment.

Data drift: the distribution of input data changes.
Concept drift: the relationship between input data and the target changes.
Process change: forms, definitions, IT systems, or data collection rules change.
Source quality change: the number of missing, delayed, or erroneous records increases.

A change in data distribution does not automatically mean model degradation, but it should trigger an analysis if it is relevant to the given application.

Example scheme:







Signal
Possible response




Increase in missing input data

Thresholds must be defined for a specific application. There is no single universal error level appropriate for all statistical processes.

title: Validation and monitoring of AI systems
text:
12 12. Example: Tourist imputation model
A model predicts the number of tourists in accommodation establishments.

Situation: it achieves good quality in a stable period.
Problem: after a change in market conditions, it systematically overestimates the results.

The team should take the following steps:

Check the input data. Has its distribution or quality changed?
Compare errors with previous periods. Is the degradation significant and systematic?
Break down the results. By season, region, and type of facility.
Evaluate the possibility of further use. Can the model still be used?
Consider corrective action. Retraining or changing the method.
Perform validation before approving the new version.

Automatic retraining should not in itself mean automatic release of the model to production.
If a change is significant (e.g., system functionality or scope changes), the review should be updated, and the new version should undergo re-approval.

title: Validation and monitoring of AI systems
text:
13 13. Accountability, documentation, and review
Validation and monitoring require clearly defined roles and a decision trail.

Accountability: assign persons to monitor and maintain the model throughout its life cycle and agree on rules for transferring responsibility from development to production.
Documentation: record assumptions, data, data splits, hyperparameters, random seed, software versions, results, and uncertainty measures.
Audit trail: record changes to the model, data, and configuration.
Fitness for purpose check: continuously compare quality with previously established success criteria and periodically review the project scope.

Example review process (Statistics Canada):

Self-assessment by the team using a checklist.
Peer review: ethical and methodological, by independent experts, and optionally also a code review.
Scientific committee: approval and recommendations, especially for new methods or key statistical programs.
Publication of the review report or its summary.

Answer the following questions:

Why might the overall accuracy not reveal the problem?
What metrics and breakdowns should be analyzed?
How can a data change be distinguished from model degradation?
When should re-validation be performed?

text:

Validation is a process, not a one-time test.
The evaluation method must correspond to the actual application of the model.
Monitoring should cover both data and output quality.
Changes in operating conditions may require re-validation.
Every new model version should be subject to control proportionate to the risk.
Test metrics do not replace statistical quality indicators for data users.
Validation covers the entire process and technical reliability, not just the model.
Accountability, documentation, and independent review are prerequisites for reliability.

title: AI Governance
text:
AI governance encompasses the rules, roles, procedures, and control mechanisms that determine how an organization selects, deploys, uses, and oversees AI solutions.
The goal is not solely to limit risk. Good governance also helps select valuable use cases, rationally utilize resources, and maintain process quality.



In official statistics, the following are particularly important:

trust in results;
data confidentiality and security;
independence and impartiality;
quality of statistical methods;
accountability for published information.




The foundation is the Framework on Responsible AI for Official Statistics from October 2025. It was developed by a group of experts from statistical offices and international organizations (including Statistics Canada, INSEE, Eurostat, UNECE) operating within the HLG-MOS.
Its goal is simple: to help agencies apply AI responsibly, i.e., in accordance with the values of official statistics.



AI helps deliver statistics faster and in greater detail, but it also carries risks: algorithmic bias, privacy breaches, and loss of public trust.
The framework emphasizes three things:

people are accountable for AI, not the system;
a balance between automation and human oversight is needed;
responsible AI is more than checking boxes in a report.











Principle
In short




Ethical purpose and public good
AI serves people and the environment, does no harm


Accountability
It is clear who is responsible for the system and its outputs


Transparency and explainability
System operation can be understood and verified


Fairness
The system does not discriminate or perpetuate bias


Privacy and security
Data and models are protected


Validity and robustness
Results are reliable and stable over time






The framework proposes three tools:

Guidelines: concrete actions derived from the principles.
Checklist: project self-assessment by its owner.
Review: evaluation by independent reviewers or a committee.

Together, these tools make up practical AI governance, which is the focus of the following sections.

section: 2 2. From a single experiment to an organizational solution
text:
2 2. From a single experiment to an organizational solution
Several stages of maturity in an AI application must be distinguished:

Experiment: we check if the solution can be useful.
Prototype: we evaluate performance on specific data and in a limited environment.
Pilot: we test the solution in conditions close to real ones.
Deployment: the solution is approved for a specific use.
Maintenance: we monitor quality, security, and changes.
Retirement: we stop using it when it is no longer justified or safe.

The success of an experiment does not automatically mean readiness for production deployment.
The framework identifies three points at which it is worth pausing:

early-stage impact assessment (when identifying business needs), on which the level of project requirements depends;
transfer of accountability upon transition from development to deployment and production, according to a pre-established procedure;
formal review upon transition from prototype to production version, which is exactly when the success of an experiment could be mistakenly considered readiness for deployment.

A central AI applications register is a useful tool.
Example fields:



Field

The register should cover a scope justified by the organization’s needs, and the information contained therein must be updated.
As a supplement, additional fields arising from the framework recommendations could be considered:

data owner and provenance (where it comes from, how it was aggregated, who is responsible for it), including information on third-party data;
model and code version along with a reference to the change audit trail;

environmental impact (estimated energy and carbon footprint), if the application requires large models.

title: AI Governance
text:
5 5. Pre-deployment risk assessment
Before starting a project, it is worth answering the following questions:

What problem is AI supposed to solve?
Is the solution necessary, or is a simpler method sufficient?
What data will be used?
What could be the consequences of an erroneous result?
Could errors affect specific groups or regions?
Can the result be verified?
Who will oversee the system’s operation?
What conditions must be met for the deployment to be permissible?

The result of the assessment should lead to a decision: continue, modify, limit the scope, or abandon the solution.
The framework clarifies how to conduct such an assessment:

it is done early, at the stage of understanding needs, and requirements are adjusted to the risk level, distinguishing high-risk systems from low or minimal risk ones;
it includes risk assessment for individuals, groups, organizations, and society and, when necessary, a privacy impact assessment;
it requires identifying stakeholders (users and those affected by the system), agreeing on goals with them, and indicating groups that may suffer harm;
it is worthwhile to gather relevant regulations regarding equal treatment;
in some jurisdictions, structured tools are used, e.g., the Canadian Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA), whose tier indicates whether the project requires an audit or peer review.

title: AI Governance
section: 6 6. Minimal life cycle for managing an AI application
text:
6 6. Minimal life cycle for managing an AI application
Example life cycle:

Idea submission and goal definition.
Preliminary value and risk assessment.
Verification of data and tool permissibility.
Design and preparation of the solution.
Validation and documentation.
Approval by appropriate roles.
Deployment and monitoring.
Periodic reviews and reassessment.
Update or retirement of the solution.

For a simple auxiliary application, the procedure can be lighter than for a system affecting statistical production. The key, however, is that the differentiation criteria are established and justified.

6.1 Example of proportionate requirements








Risk level
Example application
Example requirements




Low
Editing draft texts without confidential data
Rules of use, brief register entry, user responsibility for verifying the result


Medium
Auxiliary tool for a team, results checked before use
Risk assessment, documented validation, designated owner, periodic review


High
Model influencing numbers published in official statistics
Full risk assessment, independent review, committee approval, monitoring, and retirement plan





6.2 Example of pre-approval review (Statistics Canada)
The review is a checkpoint during the transition from prototype to production. The framework describes it in four steps:

Preparation: confirming that the project requires a review, obtaining management support, selecting independent reviewers, and checking for potential conflicts of interest.
Technical and ethical review: reviewers analyze the documentation and the system, use a checklist filled out by the team, and prepare a report with justified recommendations.
Scientific committee: the team presents the project together with the review results, and the committee considers the report when deciding on launching the system. For new methods or key statistical programs, approval by an expert committee is recommended.
Publication: the report, or its summary if full disclosure is restricted, is published. The review should be updated after significant changes in functionality or scope.

The checklist is meant to support reviewers but does not limit their assessment. Code review can be an optional step and does not replace methodological review.

AI governance should cover the entire life cycle of AI.
Rules must balance the capacity for innovation with the protection of quality, confidentiality, and trust.
The applications register facilitates control and review of deployments.
The level of control should be proportionate to the risk.
Responsible deployment requires the collaboration of methodology, technology, security, and management.
Accountability lies with people and institutions, not the system.
Responsible AI is a process, not a formality in documentation.
Independent review upon transition to production increases the credibility of deployments.

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
Artificial intelligence is not a single technology or a single algorithm. It encompasses a variety of methods that can be used, among other things, to predict values, recognize patterns, classify information, generate text, and support work with documents and code.
In official statistics, the appropriate choice of technology should stem from the nature of the problem. A different method will be suitable for forecasting tourist numbers, another for assigning classification codes to activity descriptions, and yet another for searching for information in methodological documentation.
The objective of this module is to organize the most important concepts and show how to evaluate the usefulness of AI and ML without assuming that a more complex model is automatically better.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
2.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a broad category of technologies that enable systems to perform tasks requiring specific cognitive capabilities, such as recognizing patterns, interpreting language, reasoning, or generating content.
The term AI covers various approaches, ranging from rule-based systems to modern models trained on large datasets.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
2.3 Deep Learning
Deep learning utilizes multi-layer neural networks. It is particularly useful for tasks that require processing complex data, such as text, images, audio, or large sets of unstructured information.
However, this does not mean that neural networks are the best choice for every problem. For small tabular datasets, classical statistical methods or decision trees may be easier to validate and equally effective.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
2.5 Large Language Models (LLMs)
Large Language Models (LLMs) are models trained on massive datasets of text and other data, depending on the architecture. They generate text or other outputs based on context and learned relationships.
An LLM can help write R code, but it does not guarantee that the code correctly implements statistical assumptions. It can also create non-existent references to publications or misinterpret results.
Most open-source and commercial LLMs have been trained primarily on English-language texts. When working in Polish, a higher tokenization rate occurs – the same sentence in Polish is split into a larger number of tokens (subwords/word fragments) than in English. This results in:

higher processing costs;
extended response generation times;
risk of grammatical errors and the unreflective transfer of concepts from foreign legal and statistical systems.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
2.6 Prompt Engineering
Prompt engineering is the art and technique of precisely formulating input instructions for generative models to obtain accurate, consistent, and safe responses.
In official statistics, it is recommended to use the repeatable Role–Task–Context–Format (RTCF) framework:

    T --> C[3. Context]
    C --> E[4. Examples ]
    E --> F[5. Format]
