Role: Giving the model the appropriate perspective.
Task: Precisely defining the objective.
Context: Providing background information, survey description, time period, and constraints.
Examples (Few-shot): Including 1–2 benchmark examples of a correctly performed task.
Format: Specifying the expected structure.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
2.7 RAG – Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines a generative model with an information retrieval mechanism across specific documents or a knowledge base.
For example, an assistant can search for passages from approved methodological instructions and prepare an answer based on them.
RAG can facilitate citing sources and reduce the reliance of the answer solely on the model’s parametric knowledge, but it does not eliminate errors in retrieval, interpretation, or content generation.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
3.1 Supervised Learning
The model learns on data containing examples of inputs and the expected output.
Example: a dataset of business activity descriptions where each description has a correct classification code assigned to it.
The goal is to train the model to assign codes to new descriptions.
Typical tasks:

regression – predicting a numerical value;
classification – assigning an observation to a category.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
3.2 Unsupervised Learning
The model searches for underlying structure in data without using a previously assigned target variable.
Examples:

grouping entities with similar characteristics;
identifying unusual clusters and anomalies in large datasets;
exploring and reducing the dimensionality of multivariate datasets.

The result of clustering does not necessarily align with natural or official statistical categories. Interpreting clusters requires domain knowledge.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
3.3 Semi-Supervised Learning and Active Learning
In official statistics, obtaining a fully labeled dataset (e.g., manually coded descriptions of occupations or business activities) can be very time-consuming and expensive.
Semi-Supervised Learning: Combines a small number of labeled examples with a very large unlabeled dataset. The model leverages the structure of unlabeled data to improve classification precision.
Active Learning: The algorithm identifies records for which it has the lowest prediction confidence and routes only those difficult edge cases for manual coding by a human expert. As a result, the expert verifies only a fraction of the data while the model continuously improves its performance.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
3.4 Reinforcement Learning
The model learns an action strategy based on feedback regarding the outcomes of its actions.
It is not the first-choice method for typical tasks in official statistics, such as classification, imputation, or forecasting. However, it may appear in more complex optimization and interactive systems.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
3.5 Ensemble Learning
Ensemble learning involves combining predictions from multiple distinct machine learning models (e.g., decision trees in Random Forest or Gradient Boosting methods) to obtain a single, more stable, and accurate result.
Application: This is a standard and highly effective practice in official statistics for data imputation tasks as well as automatic detection of errors and anomalies.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
3.6 Generative Models
Generative models learn to produce new examples, content, or data representations.
In official statistics, a clear distinction must be made between text generation by LLMs and synthetic data generation. These are different applications requiring distinct evaluation criteria.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
7.1 Overfitting
The model fits too closely to the nuances of the training set, including random noise that will not recur in new data.
As a result, it achieves excellent performance on training data but significantly worse results on out-of-sample observations.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
7.2 Data Leakage
Information that would not be available at the actual time of prediction, or that indirectly reveals the target variable, enters the training or feature engineering process.
Example: A model predicting March outcomes uses a feature calculated from April data, which would not yet be available at the time of forecasting. Consequently, testing artificially inflates the model’s perceived accuracy.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
7.3 Data Distribution Shift (Concept / Data Drift)
Relationships that existed in the past can change over time. Economic, regulatory, technological changes, as well as shifts in respondent behavior, influence this.
A model trained on historical periods may require re-evaluation when the data generation or collection process changes. Therefore, deployed models require continuous monitoring and periodic retraining to maintain forecast accuracy under new conditions.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
9.1 Practice 1: Model Selection
Bad: Selecting a model solely based on algorithm popularity or a single, coincidental result.
Good: Comparing several well-justified methods on the same properly prepared and representative test set.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
9.2 Practice 2: Using LLMs for Coding
Bad: Uncritically accepting AI-generated code simply because it executes without errors.
Good: Reviewing underlying logic, testing on known test cases, checking edge conditions, and comparing results against expectations.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
9.3 Practice 3: Interpreting Results
Bad: Assuming that a variable with high importance in a predictive model automatically explains the actual root cause of a phenomenon.
Good: Clearly distinguishing predictive importance (correlation) from statistical interpretation and rigorous causal inference.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
9.4 Practice 4: Choosing Complexity Level
Bad: Deploying a complex neural network when a significantly simpler model delivers similar result quality.
Good: Considering quality, maintenance cost, interpretability, infrastructure requirements, and validation capabilities.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Module 2. AI and ML – Opportunities and Limitations
text:
10.1 Proposed Solution
Dictionary rules can be transparent and effective for unambiguous descriptions, but handle ambiguity and linguistic diversity poorly.
An ML model can learn more complex patterns, but requires quality control of labels, sample representativeness, and performance verification on new data.
A generative model can additionally provide rationales, but these should not be treated as independent proof of code correctness.
The test set should be strictly separated from data used for training and tuning. Evaluation should be conducted using appropriate classification metrics and error analysis. Unambiguous cases and low-confidence predictions should be routed to human experts for verification.
The final choice should result from comparing quality, costs, and process requirements.
crumbs: 02. Fundamentals of AI and Machine Learning

title: Studia przypadków
Studia przypadków
text:
2.1 Sytuacja
Zespół statystyczny opracowuje model uczenia maszynowego, który ma służyć do przygotowywania wstępnych szacunków liczby turystów korzystających z obiektów noclegowych. Dane za ostatni miesiąc są niekompletne, ponieważ nie wszystkie jednostki przekazały sprawozdania.
Model wykorzystuje historyczne dane o turystyce, informacje o sezonowości, lokalizacji obiektów oraz wcześniejszych wartościach badanego zjawiska.
Wyniki modelu są obiecujące w okresach stabilnych, ale w czasie nagłych zmian popytu model ma tendencję do zawyżania lub zaniżania szacunków.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
2.2 Główne ryzyka

Nadmierne zaufanie do wyników modelu.
Niewystarczające uwzględnienie nietypowych zdarzeń.
Wykorzystanie danych, które nie byłyby dostępne w momencie sporządzania rzeczywistego szacunku.
Brak informacji o niepewności wyniku.
Trudność w wyjaśnieniu różnic między szacunkiem a późniejszym wynikiem badania.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
2.3 Pytania do dyskusji

Jakie dane powinny być dostępne w chwili generowania szacunku?
Jak sprawdzić, czy model nie korzysta pośrednio z informacji o przyszłości?
Jakie wyniki należy porównać z modelem: poprzedni miesiąc, analogiczny miesiąc poprzedniego roku czy prosty model sezonowy?
Czy użytkownik końcowy powinien otrzymać jeden szacunek, czy również informację o jego niepewności?
Kiedy wynik powinien zostać przekazany do dodatkowej weryfikacji?

title: Studia przypadków
text:
2.4 Rekomendowane działania

Zastosować walidację kroczącą w czasie (rolling-origin validation).
Porównać model z prostymi metodami referencyjnymi.
Ocenić błędy dla różnych okresów, regionów i typów obiektów.
Przeanalizować zachowanie modelu podczas nietypowych zdarzeń.
Dokumentować ograniczenia oraz zasady akceptacji wyników.
Pozostawić odpowiedzialność za zatwierdzenie szacunku po stronie upoważnionych pracowników.

Wniosek: model może wspierać przygotowanie wstępnych szacunków, ale jego przydatność należy oceniać w warunkach zbliżonych do rzeczywistego procesu produkcyjnego.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
3.1 Sytuacja
Pracownik chce wykorzystać publicznie dostępne narzędzie generatywnej AI do przygotowania kodu analizującego dane jednostkowe. Wkleja do rozmowy fragment zbioru zawierający identyfikatory jednostek, lokalizacje oraz wybrane cechy opisowe.
Narzędzie generuje poprawny kod, ale pracownik nie sprawdził zasad przetwarzania danych przez usługę.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
3.2 Główne ryzyka

Ujawnienie informacji chronionych.
Przekazanie danych do zewnętrznego dostawcy bez odpowiedniej podstawy i upoważnienia.
Naruszenie zasad bezpieczeństwa organizacji.
Brak kontroli nad przechowywaniem i dalszym wykorzystaniem przesłanych informacji.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
3.3 Pytania do dyskusji

Czy dane można przekazać do narzędzia AI tylko dlatego, że są potrzebne do rozwiązania zadania?
Czy usunięcie nazw i identyfikatorów zawsze zapewnia anonimowość?
Jak można uzyskać pomoc w napisaniu kodu bez przekazywania danych?
Kto powinien zatwierdzać wykorzystanie zewnętrznych narzędzi AI?

title: Studia przypadków
text:
3.4 Rekomendowane działania

Korzystać wyłącznie z narzędzi dopuszczonych przez organizację do danego rodzaju informacji.
Nie przekazywać danych poufnych bez odpowiedniej podstawy, oceny bezpieczeństwa i upoważnienia.
Zastępować rzeczywiste rekordy danymi syntetycznymi lub minimalnymi przykładami, gdy jest to wystarczające.
Sprawdzać warunki przetwarzania danych i ustawienia usługi.
W razie podejrzenia ujawnienia informacji postępować zgodnie z procedurą incydentową.

Wniosek: użyteczność narzędzia nie znosi obowiązku ochrony danych. Przed użyciem AI należy ocenić zarówno charakter danych, jak i środowisko przetwarzania.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
4.1 Sytuacja
Model przewidujący wartość badanego zjawiska osiąga dobre wyniki w skali całego kraju. Po analizie szczegółowej okazuje się jednak, że błędy są znacznie większe w małych gminach i regionach o niestandardowej strukturze gospodarczej.
W zbiorze treningowym dominowały obserwacje z dużych jednostek.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
4.2 Główne ryzyka

Nierównomierna jakość wyników dla różnych grup i obszarów.
Niedostateczna reprezentacja rzadkich przypadków.
Ukrywanie lokalnych błędów przez dobre wyniki zagregowane.
Podejmowanie decyzji na podstawie wyników, które nie są równie wiarygodne we wszystkich obszarach.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
4.3 Pytania do dyskusji

Czy dobry wynik ogólny wystarcza do uznania modelu za odpowiedni?
Jakie grupy i obszary powinny zostać uwzględnione w ocenie?
Czy większy błąd w małych jednostkach jest akceptowalny?
Jakie rozwiązania można zastosować bez sztucznego wyrównywania danych?

title: Studia przypadków
text:
4.4 Rekomendowane działania

Obliczać miary błędu dla istotnych grup i poziomów agregacji.
Sprawdzić liczebności obserwacji w poszczególnych grupach.
Zidentyfikować obszary, dla których model działa słabiej.
Rozważyć dodatkowe cechy, odpowiednią metodę modelowania lub odrębne podejście dla wybranych grup.
Opisać ograniczenia modelu i monitorować je po wdrożeniu.

Wniosek: jakość modelu należy oceniać nie tylko globalnie, ale również z uwzględnieniem zastosowania i grup, dla których wyniki będą wykorzystywane.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
5.1 Sytuacja
Pracownik wykorzystuje model językowy do przygotowania opisu wyników badania statystycznego. Tekst jest płynny i przekonujący, ale zawiera błędną interpretację jednego wskaźnika oraz przyczynowe wyjaśnienie zmiany, którego nie potwierdzają dane.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
5.2 Główne ryzyka

Wygenerowanie nieprawdziwych informacji.
Pomylenie korelacji z zależnością przyczynową.
Zmiana znaczenia wskaźnika podczas upraszczania tekstu.
Przekazanie błędnego komunikatu odbiorcom statystyki publicznej.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
5.3 Pytania do dyskusji

Które elementy opisu można sprawdzić automatycznie?
Jak zweryfikować interpretację wskaźników?
Czy płynność tekstu świadczy o jego poprawności?
Kto odpowiada za ostateczną wersję publikowanego opisu?

title: Studia przypadków
text:
5.4 Rekomendowane działania

Przekazywać modelowi definicje wskaźników i zatwierdzone wyniki, o ile zasady bezpieczeństwa na to pozwalają.
Weryfikować każdą wartość liczbową, jednostkę, okres i porównanie.
Oddzielać opis obserwowanych zmian od hipotez dotyczących ich przyczyn.
Wymagać przeglądu merytorycznego przed publikacją.
Nie traktować tekstu wygenerowanego przez AI jako źródła dowodów.

Wniosek: generatywna AI może wspierać redakcję, ale nie zastępuje weryfikacji statystycznej i odpowiedzialności autora.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
6.1 Sytuacja
Model działa poprawnie w testach, ale po kilku miesiącach jego błędy rosną. Zmieniła się struktura badanej populacji, a część cech wejściowych jest zbierana według zmodyfikowanej procedury.
Nie ustanowiono formalnego procesu monitorowania jakości modelu.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
6.2 Główne ryzyka

Pogorszenie jakości danych wejściowych.
Zmiana rozkładów cech lub relacji między cechami a wynikiem.
Wykorzystywanie modelu poza zakresem, w którym został zwalidowany.
Brak jednoznacznych kryteriów wycofania modelu.

title: Studia przypadków
text:
6.3 Pytania do dyskusji

Jakie miary i wskaźniki należy monitorować?
Jak odróżnić naturalną zmienność od trwałego pogorszenia jakości?
Kiedy należy ponownie wytrenować model?
Kto powinien zatwierdzić nową wersję?

title: Studia przypadków
text:
6.4 Rekomendowane działania

Monitorować jakość danych wejściowych i dostępne miary błędu.
Ustalić progi ostrzegawcze i kryteria interwencji.
Rejestrować wersje danych, kodu, modelu i konfiguracji.
Ponownie walidować model po istotnych zmianach.
Zapewnić możliwość powrotu do poprzedniej wersji lub metody referencyjnej.

Wniosek: walidacja przed wdrożeniem nie wystarcza. Odpowiedzialne wykorzystanie AI wymaga monitorowania i zarządzania zmianą przez cały okres działania systemu.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
text:
The integration of generative and classical artificial intelligence in statistical organizations creates enormous opportunities to increase agility, efficiency, and innovation. At the same time, it brings significant risks and management challenges that—without strong frameworks and clear transparency mechanisms—can undermine public trust, transparency, and accountability.
In official statistics, the outcome of AI-supported processes should be not only useful, but also explainable, verifiable, and reproducible.
If an AI model supports key production stages, such as classification, imputation, quality control, or data analysis, one must be able to answer the questions:

What problem are we solving?
Why was AI chosen instead of a simpler method?
What data was the solution developed and tested on?
What are the limitations of the model?
Who approves the results?
How can the analysis be reproduced?

Transparency does not mean that every user must know the mathematical details of the model. It means they receive information appropriate to their role and decisions made.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
text:
2 2. What needs to be documented?
To manage technological and operational risk, the documentation of AI processes must be systematic and comprehensive. The scope of collected information should always be proportional to the level of risk and criticality of a given application.



Area
Sample information




Objective
Statistical problem and justification for using AI


Data
Sources, time frame, population, limitations


Data preparation
Cleaning, transformations, imputations


Model
Algorithm type, version, parameters


Training
Data split, validation, tuning method


Results
Metrics, errors, comparison with baseline


Limitations
Cases where the model may perform worse


Supervision
Responsible person, control and approval method


Operation
Production version, monitoring, withdrawal conditions


Reproducibility
Code, dependencies, random seed, run date



The scope of documentation should be proportional to the risk and importance of the application.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
text:
3 3. Model documentation vs. process documentation
Model documentation focuses on the technical dimension: it describes the algorithm itself, input data structure, parameters, obtained quality metrics, and identified mathematical limitations. Process documentation is operational and organizational in nature: it describes the exact place in statistical production where the model’s output is used, who checks its correctness and under what rules, and what steps should be taken if an error or anomaly is detected.
Technical documentation alone is not sufficient if it is unknown where in the statistical process the model’s result is used.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
text:
5 5. Explainability and interpretation
In the processes of implementing AI in statistical offices, three levels of explaining system operation should be clearly distinguished:

global explanation — describes the general logic of the model’s operation in relation to the entire dataset. It answers the question which features (explanatory variables) have the greatest significance for prediction on a macro scale.
local explanation — focuses on a single observation (e.g., a specific household, enterprise, or region). It explains why the system made a particular decision in that specific case.
operational description — concerns understanding how the obtained result translates into the final statistical process.

High variable importance in the model is not synonymous with a causal relationship – predictive dependence does not constitute proof of causality. In the case of advanced modeling structures, it is worth using explanatory methods such as permutation importance or SHAP, but the results obtained using them also require careful interpretation.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
section: 6 6. Example of good and bad practice
text:
6 6. Example of good and bad practice
Bad practice
“The model works well. AI was used to automatically fill in missing data.”
Problem: lack of information on source data, validation methods, actual prediction quality, algorithm limitations, and human supervision procedures.
Better practice
“A verified Random Forest model was used to generate imputation proposals for missing values. The model quality was systematically evaluated on a held-out test sample using historical actual data, and the results were compared with the previous baseline method broken down by key regions. Imputed values are appropriately marked in the system (imputation flag), and their final approval is subject to expert control in accordance with the internal quality procedure of the statistical process.”
The above description constitutes a model example of structuring information about the process, rather than a declaration of the results of a specific empirical study.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
text:
7 7. Exercise
A team implemented a model for the automatic assignment of economic activity codes based on text descriptions.
Prepare a list of five pieces of information that should be included in the documentation before using the results in the production process.
Then answer:

What errors may be difficult to detect?
What information should the result user receive?
Who should approve model changes?

## 8. Checklist

The purpose of the AI application is unambiguous.
Data sources and preparation are described.
Quality metrics and the baseline method are documented.
Limitations and risks are transparent.
Results can be reproduced in a specified environment.
It is clear who is responsible for control and approval.
Model changes and versions are logged.

title: Transparency and Documentation of AI Systems
text:
8 9. Key Conclusions

Documentation as the foundation of quality: Documentation is an integral part of the quality of the statistical process, not an optional project addition.
Verifiability of results: Every result generated by the model should be independently verifiable through transparent testing procedures and data access.
Tailoring explainability: The degree of model explainability must be strictly adapted to the knowledge level and specific needs of the end-user.
Transparency of limitations: The transparency of the analytical process requires clear communication regarding model limitations and associated uncertainty.
Reliability of validation: A model should not be assigned a reliability higher than what is unambiguously confirmed by objective and independent validation results.

title: Glossary
text:
1 How to use the glossary
The glossary explains terms used in the training materials. The definitions are practical in nature and adapted to the context of official statistics.


2 A
AI system
A machine-based system that, from the input data it receives, generates outputs such as predictions, recommendations, content or decisions that may influence physical or virtual environments.
Algorithm
A set of rules or operations used to solve a specific computational problem.
Anonymisation
The process of transforming personal data so that the person to whom the data relate can no longer be identified by means reasonably likely to be used. The effectiveness of anonymisation requires an assessment of the risk of re-identification.
Automation
The performance of tasks by a system without the need to carry out each step manually. Automation does not have to use AI.


3 B
Bias
A systematic tendency that leads to particular errors or unjustified differences in results. It may stem from, among other things, the data, the design of the model, the way of measurement or the application.
Big data
Datasets whose scale, variety or velocity of arrival creates particular requirements for storage and analysis.
Black box
A term for a system whose internal workings, or the way it arrives at a result, are difficult for the user to understand.


4 C
Concept drift
A change in the relationship between the input features and the predicted outcome. It can cause a deterioration in model quality even when there are no obvious changes in the input data itself.
Cross-validation
A model evaluation method that involves repeatedly training and testing the model on different subsets of the data. It must be adapted to the structure of the data; in time series analysis, an ordinary random split can lead to an incorrect assessment.


5 D
Data drift
A change in the distribution of input data over time or between environments. It may, but does not have to, lead to a deterioration in model quality.
Data leakage
A situation in which, during model training or evaluation, information is used that would not be available at the time the model is actually applied, or information from a part of the data that should remain independent.


6 E
Explainability
The ability to provide understandable information about how a model arrives at its results or which factors influence its behaviour.
Explainable AI (XAI)
Methods and tools that support explaining how AI models work and interpreting their results.


7 F
Feature
A variable used by the model as input information, e.g. region, month, type of facility or a value from the previous period.
Feature engineering
The process of creating, transforming and selecting the features used in modelling.


8 G
Generative AI
AI systems capable of creating new content, e.g. text, code, images or sound, on the basis of data and input instructions.
GSBPM (Generic Statistical Business Process Model)
A generic model that describes the stages of the statistical production process. It can be used to identify the points at which AI supports particular activities.


9 H
Human oversight
Organisational and technical arrangements ensuring appropriate human control over an AI system and its results.
Hyperparameters
Parameters set before training or during model configuration, e.g. the number of trees in a random forest or the depth of a tree.


10 I
Imputation
Filling in missing values in a dataset using a specific method. It may use simple rules, statistical methods or machine learning models.
Individual-level data
Data relating to individual observation units, e.g. enterprises, households or accommodation establishments.
Interpretability
The degree to which a human can understand the relationships between the input data and the model’s results. In practice the term is sometimes used interchangeably with explainability, although the two concepts may be distinguished.


11 L
Large Language Model (LLM)
A large-scale language model trained on extensive text datasets and, depending on the architecture, other data. It can generate text, answer questions and support work with code.
Leakage
See data leakage.
Learning algorithm
The procedure by which a model fits its parameters to the training data.


12 M
Machine learning (ML)
A field of AI comprising methods that learn patterns from data and use them for prediction, classification or other tasks.
MAE (Mean Absolute Error)
The average of the absolute differences between actual and predicted values. A lower value usually indicates a smaller error.
Model
A mathematical or computational representation of relationships, used to predict, classify, estimate or generate results.
Model governance
A set of activities including monitoring, documenting, approving changes and responding to problems related to the model’s performance.
Model monitoring
Regular assessment of the quality of the model’s performance after deployment, including analysis of errors, changes in the data and fitness for purpose.


13 O
Official statistics
The system of collecting, compiling, analysing and disseminating statistical data in order to inform society and institutions about social, economic, demographic and environmental phenomena.
Outlier
An observation that differs markedly from the others. It is not necessarily erroneous; it may reflect a real, rare phenomenon.
Overfitting
A situation in which a model fits the training data too closely but generalises poorly to new observations.


14 P
Precision
A term with different meanings depending on the context. In statistical estimation it may refer to the exactness of an estimate, and in classification — to the share of correct positive predictions among all positive predictions.
Privacy
The area concerned with protecting individuals and information about them. In work with data it includes, among other things, restricting access and minimising the risk of identification.
Prompt
An instruction or a set of information given to a generative model in order to obtain a specific result.


15 R
Recall (sensitivity)
In classification, the share of correctly detected positive cases among all actual positive cases.
Reproducibility
The ability to reproduce results on the basis of documented data, code, parameters, software versions and analytical procedure, taking into account possible sources of non-determinism.
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
The square root of the mean squared error. It penalises large errors more heavily than MAE. Its value is expressed in the unit of the forecast variable.


16 S
Sensitivity analysis
An examination of how results change when assumptions, parameters or input data are changed.
Synthetic data
Artificially generated data that is intended to reproduce selected properties of real data. It does not automatically guarantee the absence of disclosure risk.


17 T
Test data
Data used for an independent assessment of model quality after training has been completed and the configuration has been chosen.
Test set
Data used for the final assessment of model quality on observations not used during fitting and selection.
Training data
Data used to fit the model’s parameters.
Training set
Data used to train the model.
Transparency
Availability of information about the purpose, operation, limitations and manner of use of the system.


18 U
Uncertainty
Lack of full knowledge about a value, outcome or process. In statistical analysis it may be described by, among other things, standard errors, confidence intervals or predictive distributions.
Underfitting
A situation in which a model is too simple to capture the significant relationships present in the data.


19 V
Validation
The process of assessing whether a model meets specified requirements and is suitable for the intended use.
Validation set
Data used for model selection, hyperparameter tuning or comparison of variants during the development of a solution.
Versioning
Recording changes to data, code, models, configuration and documentation, enabling a specific version of the solution to be identified.


20 W
Workflow
An ordered sequence of activities leading to the completion of a task, e.g. preparing and publishing statistical results.


21 Important note on terminology
The meaning of some terms depends on the field and the application. In project documentation it is worth specifying how the terms that are key to the assessment of quality, risk and responsibility are understood.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
AI models learn from data that reflect specific conditions, measurement methods, and decisions made during dataset preparation. If the data do not cover all relevant situations or contain systematic errors, the model may replicate or amplify these problems.
In official statistics, it is particularly important that model quality may vary across regions, time periods, types of units, or other cross-sections relevant to the survey.
A low average error for the entire dataset does not mean the model is equally good for every part of the population. It may perform very well for numerous, typical units while making large errors for rare, seasonal, or atypical units.
The goal of this module is to teach participants how to identify sources of bias and select control methods suited to a specific application.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
section: 3.1 1. Data Do Not Cover All Relevant Cases
text:
3.1 1. Data Do Not Cover All Relevant Cases
The model learns from available observations. If specific types of units are rare or poorly represented, the model may not learn their characteristic patterns.
In analytical practice, this phenomenon leads to so-called algorithmic blind spots. Statistical and machine learning models show a strong tendency to favor majority classes, relegating rare cases to the role of informational noise. As a result, the system may generate extremely inaccurate forecasts or make erroneous decisions in atypical, crisis, or innovative situations that lacked numerous representations in the training history.
Example: a tourist volume forecasting model learns mainly from large, year-round facilities and has few examples from small, seasonal facilities. As a result, forecasts for agritourism or summer cottages will be subject to huge errors because the model does not account for the specifics of sudden demand spikes caused by weather factors or short holiday weekends.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
3.2 2. Measurement Errors
Input data may contain errors, outdated information, or values obtained using different measurement procedures.
Sources of disturbance:

Human errors: respondent mistakes, interviewer errors, typos, or omitted digits during data entry and initial editing.
System failures: faults in ICT infrastructure, databases, or telemetry systems collecting information in real time.
Evolution of standards: changes in indicator definitions, classifications, and data acquisition methods, leading to a natural break in the continuity of time series.

If these inaccuracies are systematic, the machine learning model will not only adopt them but actually reinforce them, treating the distorted signal as a business or physical rule. As a result, the algorithm may learn dependencies reflecting the specifics of data collection rather than the actual phenomenon.
For example, if the survey method was changed during a certain period and telephone interviews were conducted more frequently instead of in-person ones, the change in results may merely reflect the specifics of the new communication medium rather than a real shift in consumer attitudes, completely misleading an algorithm searching for deeper market correlations.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
3.3 3. Incomplete or Ambiguous Labels
In supervised learning, the model reproduces patterns present in the training data. If the labels are incorrect or inconsistently assigned, the result may be inconsistent.
Model quality is directly limited by the quality of the so-called “ground truth.” If the data labeling process relies on subjective expert assessments where interpretations of criteria differ among experts, the algorithm falls into the trap of conflicting signals, trying to find a common denominator where none de facto exists.
Example: similar business activity descriptions receive different codes depending on the coder or the time period. Such discrepancies confuse text classifiers, which, instead of learning the actual company profile, begin picking up random stylistic preferences of individual administrative staff.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
3.4 4. Improper Sample Selection
The training set may differ from the population or from the data on which the model will be used.
This problem is closely related to selection bias. If the dataset was collected under specific conditions (e.g., exclusively in large urban agglomerations or during a strong economic boom), the sample becomes unrepresentative. Deploying such a model in an environment with a different demographic or macroeconomic structure leads to a drastic drop in its effectiveness.
Not only sizes are important, but also the range of variability, the structure of units, and the conditions under which observations are generated.
This means that even a giant dataset with low structural diversity will prove less valuable than a smaller, yet perfectly balanced sample reflecting the full spectrum of extreme market scenarios in which the system will have to operate.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
3.5 5. Inappropriate Objective Function
The model may optimize the average error even though specific types of mistakes are particularly important in a given application.
Standard loss functions (such as mean squared error) treat every error symmetrically. In business or medical reality, the costs of false positive and false negative errors differ drastically (e.g., the cost of missing a cancer diagnosis is incomparably higher than the cost of an additional examination for a healthy patient). An improper choice of the optimization criterion will make the model mathematically perfect, but business-wise useless or even harmful.
Example: minimizing overall error may favor fitting large units if their values dominate the evaluation criterion. In such a situation, the algorithm will ignore niche yet strategically crucial small entities, focusing all its computing power on perfectly forecasting the behavior of market giants, which distorts the overall portfolio picture.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
3.6 6. Changing Conditions Over Time
Relationships present in historical data may cease to hold after changes in the economic situation, survey methodology, respondent behavior, or data collection methods.
This phenomenon, known as model aging or concept drift, affects almost every system deployed in a dynamic environment. The market, legal, and technical environment evolves continuously, causing historical patterns to lose their predictive power in favor of new, hitherto unknown cause-and-effect mechanisms.
A model that was appropriate in previous years does not necessarily retain the same quality in subsequent periods.
This requires the implementation of permanent prediction quality monitoring, cyclical system retraining on fresh data, and readiness to quickly rebuild the feature architecture whenever macroeconomic environmental parameters undergo a fundamental breakthrough.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
4.1 Alternative Data
Data originating from the internet, mobile devices, digital platforms, or other alternative sources can increase the range of available information.
The process of collecting such data can generate selection bias. For example, data from online platforms concern solely their users, not the entire population. Drawing conclusions about a broader scale based on them requires evaluating coverage, the source of selection, and the application of corrections. A large sample size does not automatically guarantee its representativeness.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
6.3 Classification Analysis
Evaluating classification models requires a detailed analysis of the confusion matrix and metrics such as precision, recall, and the F1-score.
If the categories have different sizes, overall accuracy alone can be misleading. A model may classify the most frequent category well while poorly recognizing rare classes.
The selection of evaluation metrics should take into account the specifics of the problem and the business or practical consequences of individual types of errors.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.1 1. Understand the Data Generation Mechanism
Before training a model, it must be determined how the data were collected, what they measure, what limitations they have, and which units may be underrepresented.

Historical and social context: Data often reflect past decision-making processes that may have been subject to human biases or exclusions.
Sample analysis: It is worth thoroughly examining whether the data collection process favored specific groups (e.g., due to access to technology, geographical location, or socio-economic status), which could lead to distorted prediction results.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.2 2. Improve Label Quality
In classification tasks, it is worth defining consistent coding rules, analyzing ambiguous cases, and controlling the consistency of labels.

Standardization and guidelines: Developing precise class definitions and clear instructions for data labelers minimizes subjectivity in interpretation.
Consistency verification: Introducing independent quality control (e.g., through multi-stage labeling of the same samples by different experts and measuring agreement coefficients, such as Cohen’s Kappa) allows errors to be detected and corrected at an early stage.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.3 3. Ensure Proper Data Splitting
Test data should reflect the conditions of future model use.
In time series analysis, the split must respect chronology. Random splitting of observations can lead to an overly optimistic evaluation if future information indirectly leaks into the training process.

Avoiding data leakage: In classic datasets, care must be taken to ensure that the features of the training and testing sets are completely disjointed (e.g., avoiding situations where data for the same person are in both sets).
Representativeness of the production environment: The validation set should simulate real operational scenarios, including rarer events and atypical market or usage conditions.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.4 4. Evaluate Results Across Relevant Slices
In addition to global metrics, errors should be analyzed for methodologically important groups.

Algorithmic fairness: The global accuracy of a model can mask serious errors committed against smaller population subgroups (e.g., demographic minorities or specific customer segments).
Detailed indicators: It is worth calculating quality metrics (such as recall, specificity, or precision) separately for each important slice to ensure that the model operates fairly and stably across all analyzed segments.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.5 5. Consider Alternative Methods
If a model performs poorly in a specific area, additional features, a different method, a separate model, expert rules, or referring some cases to manual verification should be considered.

Hybrid decision-making approach In high-risk situations or where data are scarce, combining machine learning models with hard business rules can significantly increase the safety and correctness of decisions.
Hybrid decision-making approach For cases with a high degree of algorithmic uncertainty, a mechanism for automatically routing cases for verification by qualified specialists should be implemented.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.6 6. Document Limitations
Documentation should indicate under what conditions the model was evaluated, where its quality is lower, and what limitations should be taken into account when interpreting the results.

Model Cards: Creating transparent reports containing the training data profile, optimal operating ranges, and known risks facilitates responsible use of the technology by business and technical stakeholders.
Transparency of assumptions: Transparent presentation of technological limitations prevents over-reliance on results (so-called automation bias) and facilitates the auditing of artificial intelligence systems.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
8.7 7. Monitor Quality Post-Deployment
Data distribution and model quality can change over time. Therefore, analysis should not end at the pre-production validation stage.

Detecting shifts in distribution (Data Drift & Concept Drift): Regularly tracking statistics of incoming data allows deviations from the conditions under which the model was trained to be noticed in time.
Cyclic retraining: Maintaining high predictive quality requires continuous supervision, periodic re-evaluation of system effectiveness, and adapting it to changing business and social environments.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
9.1 Case A. Forecasting for Regions
Bad practice
The model achieves low error nationwide. The team does not analyze regional results and considers the model good enough.
Good practice
The team compares errors between regions, analyzes the direction of deviations, sample sizes, and the specifics of local data. They also check the impact of errors on national and regional aggregates.
Conclusion: global quality does not replace quality analysis across relevant slices.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
section: 9.2 Case B. Classification of Rare Categories
text:
9.2 Case B. Classification of Rare Categories
Bad practice
The model achieves high overall accuracy because it correctly classifies the most frequent categories. Rare categories are almost always assigned to the dominant class.
Good practice
The team analyzes precision, recall, and the confusion matrix for individual classes. They introduce expert control for rare and ambiguous categories.
Conclusion: a global metric can mask a model’s lack of utility for rare categories.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
9.3 Case C. Alternative Data
Bad practice
The team treats a large number of internet observations as sufficient proof of population representativeness.
Good practice
The team analyzes coverage, selection mechanisms, differences from available reference sources, and the possibility of correcting results.
Conclusion: dataset size does not eliminate the selection problem.

title: Module 4. Bias, Fairness and Representativeness
text:
10.1 Proposed solution
Overall accuracy alone is not sufficient. Results for individual categories must be analyzed, especially recall, precision, and types of errors.
It is worth separating unambiguous cases from difficult ones and assessing whether rare categories have a sufficient number of examples for reliable validation.
A hybrid solution can be adopted: automatically accept cases meeting established criteria, and route the rest to an expert. Criteria should be established based on validation results rather than solely on an arbitrary confidence value returned by the model.
It should also be monitored whether the procedure causes systematic omission of specific categories.

5 5. Responsibility Matrix
For each application, it is worth determining who:

performs the task;
is accountable for the result;
consults the solution;
is informed about the decision.

The RACI matrix can be used for this purpose. Situations should be avoided where many people participate in the process, but none has a clearly assigned ultimate responsibility for its outcome.
The acronym RACI comes from the English names of four roles assigned to individuals or teams for each task or project stage:

R (Responsible): The person or team that actually performs the given task and carries out the assigned work.
A (Accountable): The person bearing ultimate responsibility for the outcome (there should be only one such person per task). They approve the final result and have veto power.
C (Consulted): Experts or stakeholders with whom solutions are consulted and from whom opinions and advice are gathered before key decisions are made (two-way communication).
I (Informed): Individuals who must be kept up to date on progress, decisions made, or work results, but do not take an active part in the process itself (one-way information flow).

title: Oversight and Accountability for AI
text:
6 6. Example: Automatic Imputation
The model imputes missing data on the number of tourists.
Before deployment, responsibilities must be precisely assigned:

Who approves the imputation method?
Who analyzes the validation results?
Who controls atypical predictions?
Who can trigger re-processing?
Who decides to suspend model usage?
Who approves the new version?

If the answers are exclusively “the AI team” or “the system,” the division of responsibility is too vague.

title: Oversight and Accountability for AI
text:
7 7. When is Intervention Required?
Example triggers that should initiate an intervention procedure include:

quality drops below an established threshold: performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, precision, relevance) fall below a pre-agreed acceptance level.
new data categories appear: input data begins to contain segments or formats upon which the model was not trained.
data collection methods change: sources or information acquisition procedures are modified, which may affect data drift.
the model generates atypical or implausible results: the model produces anomalies, hallucinations, or common-sense-defying answers.
a security issue is uncovered: vulnerabilities, system manipulation attempts, or privacy breach risks are detected.
results differ significantly from independent sources: model-generated results diverge significantly from verified external data or benchmarks.
a significant change occurs to the model or its purpose: architectural modifications are made or the business context of the system’s application changes.

Alarm thresholds and specific response pathways (who, what, and how quickly must be done) should be precisely established, tested, and documented prior to the official launch of the solution. This helps prevent decision-making chaos in an emergency.
